Progress report · proximity skin for robot arms

Feeling in the dark

Jay Vakil24 July – 14 August 2026weekly from here

The main result held up and is figure-ready: a proximity skin cuts crashes from 66 out of 100 tries down to 40 when the cameras cannot see the obstacle. The last three weeks went into a follow-up experiment that did not work — and the reason it failed changed how I plan to run the next one.

66% → 40% Crashes, with the obstacle hidden from the cameras p = 0.016 · 50 tries
225 tries Blur follow-up: 13.4 hours of GPU, no usable pattern negative result
±40 pts How much of a 25-try number is luck. Now measured. 50 tries is the new floor
01

What we build, in one picture

Every robot is tested in three setups: no obstacle, an obstacle the cameras can see, and an obstacle the cameras cannot see. We hide it from the camera renderer only — the physics is unchanged and the skin still feels it. That last setup is the clean version of an everyday failure: fog, dim light, a dirty lens, an obstacle the same colour as the wall.

02

The result that matters

One more thing worth flagging: the camera-only robot crashes just as much when the obstacle is fully visible to it (64% vs 66%). It never learned obstacle avoidance from the cameras at all. So the skin is not a backup sense here — it is the only sense doing avoidance.

03

What I did in these three weeks

The plan was simple: if the story is “the skin matters because cameras fail,” then break the cameras and watch what happens. I trained three camera-only robots with every training image blurred, then tested them on clear images.

04

Lessons learned

This is the useful part of the three weeks.

Lesson 1 · measurement

A low crash rate can mean “broken”, not “careful”.

The mildly-blurred robot has the fewest crashes of anything I have trained. It also almost never finishes the task — it learned to barely move. Only the strict score, did the job AND never touched anything, tells careful apart from broken.

Lesson 2 · what to trust

Training numbers did not predict what the robot did.

The prediction errors formed a perfect ladder. The behaviour didn't. The robot with the second-worst score on paper was the best robot in the room.

Lesson 3 · how much is luck

25 tries is not enough — and now I know by how much.

Below is one robot in three setups that differ only in whether an obstacle exists. Blur cannot cause that gap, so 40 points is what luck looks like at 25 tries. Everything from here uses 50 minimum.

Lesson 4 · process

Two habits, each already paid for with a lost night.

A graphics-driver mismatch let all 25 runs fail silently overnight — there is now a two-second check that refuses to start. And a 13-hour job printed an empty summary table because of a one-line bug in the part that runs last. Test the summary step before launching the long part.

06

Progress towards a paper

  • Two figures are done and real — sections 02 and 04 above. The graded 2 / 14 / 26 pattern is the single strongest thing we have, and it is new this week.
  • The headline figure is now defined: two crash curves as the cameras get worse — one flat and low with the skin, one flat and high without — with task success collapsing underneath both. It answers the question a reviewer actually asks: why add a skin if you already have cameras? Because cameras have a failure mode the skin does not, and it isn't exotic.
  • The tool for it was built and verified this week. I can now blur the cameras at test time on a finished robot, leaving the skin untouched. Same robot, same test scenarios, only camera quality changes — which removes the exact weakness that killed the blur experiment. First answer costs 12 hours of GPU.
  • Still missing before it is submittable: more than one training run per result, and a crash counter that can tell “hit the obstacle” from “brushed the wall”.
07

Blockers

  1. The crash counter is too blunt. It counts any contact with the environment. About 60 of those 66 points are the arm brushing the tight space it was told to reach into; the obstacle itself only adds about 5. I am measuring a small effect through a noisy instrument. The code already works out what it touched, then throws the name away — a five-line fix, but old runs can't be recovered, so it costs a re-run.
  2. One GPU, and tests can't run in parallel (memory). At 3.6 minutes per try, one experiment is 12–47 hours. This is the real limit on how much I can support statistically.
  3. The dataset is stuck at 105 demonstrations instead of 200 — three of four collection workers get killed for using too much memory. Fixable by running fewer, slower.
  4. Every result is a single training run. Three seeds each would turn “promising” into “defensible”, and triples the GPU time.
08

Next week

  1. Fix the crash counter so crashes are split by what was actually hit, then re-run.
  2. Run the 12-hour version of the new experiment: two robots, clear vs blurred cameras at test time, 50 tries each. Enough to see whether the two crash curves separate at all.
  3. Start repeat runs with different random seeds on the main result.
One question for you

Limited GPU means I can do either repeat-runs of the existing result or the new camera-corruption experiment first, not both. My instinct is the new experiment, because it turns one condition into a curve and that is the figure a paper needs — but repeat-runs are what make the existing number safe to publish. Which would you rather see first?
